Commenter says they appreciate SerpApi's product: it provides a machine interface to Google results that Google itself refuses to offer, plus visibility into SERPs that users should have access to.
Several commenters argue SerpApi exists only because Google doesn't offer a usable, reasonably priced search API of its own.

A commenter who hadn't heard of SerpApi before the lawsuit says that if they want a Google results API, they'll choose the one so hard for Google to block that Google had to sue. They note the advertised 'legal shield' where SerpApi assumes scraping liability for customers.

A commenter says that as more search is done programmatically on behalf of users (scripts, AI tools), people naturally end up using SerpApi or similar search APIs because 'they are great for the job.'

A user's idea: use SerpApi to save the top 10–20 links for millions of queries into a RAG database. A local LLM plus a crawler could then do web search without touching Google, refreshing the index every few months.

Critics in the thread note SerpApi doesn't obey robots.txt, unlike Google, and call that an important distinction. Another commenter characterizes SerpApi's traffic as malicious requests to google.com rather than ordinary website scraping.

A former user who used SerpApi 'many moons ago' says the most interesting part is the U.S. Legal Shield on plans (e.g., Production, $150 for 15,000 searches/month). They suspect some companies use SerpApi just for that liability shield.
Skeptics compare the Legal Shield to old SSL certificate warranties: 'pretty words, but meaningless in practice.' They see the 'unless your usage is illegal' clause as a big loophole.

Complaint about the SerpApi MCP Server: embedding the API key in the URL complicates secret management. The user asked for header-based auth configurable via an env var. (A SerpApi rep replied that Bearer auth is already supported at mcp.serpapi.com/mcp.)

After the motion to dismiss was granted, a commenter reading the motion argues Google mostly needs to fix a DRM-authorization gap in its complaint. Once it does, they don't see SerpApi prevailing 'in court or in the marketplace.'
